pages.x: The Mauryan Empire, founded by Chandragupta around 320 BC, ruled nearly all of the Indian subcontinent. Kalinga, on the east coast in what is now Odisha, grew rich from trade by sea and stayed free. Around 262 BC Chandragupta's grandson, the emperor Ashoka, marched against it.

Kalinga fought hard, but we know almost nothing of how. Nearly everything we know of the war comes from Ashoka himself. Tradition places the last battle by the Daya river, below the hill of Dhauli, where the river is said to have run red.

In an inscription carved on rock a few years later, Ashoka says that 150,000 people were carried off, 100,000 were killed and many times that number died. He says the memory filled him with sorrow and regret, words no other conqueror of the ancient world put in stone.

After Kalinga, Ashoka gave himself to dhamma, the Buddhist idea of right living: kindness to all living things, respect for parents, teachers and the poor, and tolerance of every faith. He said he would conquer from now on only by dhamma, never again by the sword.
Ashoka had his messages carved on rocks and on polished stone pillars across his empire, in local languages, and in Greek and Aramaic in the far northwest.
pages.fx: They are among the oldest readable writing in India. Their Brahmi script, mother of most Indian scripts, was deciphered again only in 1837.

pages.x: The inscriptions tell of wells dug and banyan trees planted along the roads for shade, of rest houses, of care for sick people and sick animals, and of fewer animals killed for the royal kitchen. Ashoka sent teachers of the Buddha to Sri Lanka and to the Greek kings of the west.
Four lions back to back crowned the pillar Ashoka set up at Sarnath, where the Buddha first taught. They are now the emblem of India, and the wheel carved beneath them is the wheel on its flag.

Kalinga made Ashoka that rare conqueror remembered for his regret. His support helped Buddhism spread from India to Sri Lanka and, in time, across Asia, and his picture of a ruler who governs by kindness is still honoured in India.
pts: Turned Ashoka from war to dhamma
His lions and wheel are symbols of India today
